unit.title: Market research and customer insight
unit.description: Qualitative and quantitative, primary and secondary data, sampling, survey bias, interviews, NPS, CSAT, CES

cards.definition: Surveying a subset of the population instead of everyone. To generalize, the sample must look like the population (quota or random sampling) and be big enough; 1,000 well chosen people can describe a country.
cards.example: A poll of 1,000 French adults built on quotas of age, sex, region and job.
alts: A subset of a population chosen so that its structure mirrors the whole, which lets a survey of a few people describe many.

cards.definition: Ways a survey misleads: leading questions, people saying what is socially expected, only motivated people answering, or asking about future behaviour, which people predict badly.
cards.example: Would you buy an eco-friendly product? gets 80 percent yes; actual sales are far lower.
alts: Ways a questionnaire distorts reality: leading wording, socially expected answers, self-selected respondents and questions about future behaviour.

cards.definition: A moderated discussion with 6 to 10 people to explore perceptions and words. Rich for ideas, but small and influenced by the loudest participants: never use it to measure.
cards.example: Testing three packaging concepts with young parents before a quantitative test.
alts: A moderated discussion with a handful of people to explore perceptions and vocabulary: good for ideas, never for measuring.

cards.definition: A one to one conversation about real past behaviour (the last time you bought, what you tried before) rather than opinions about the future. Five to ten good interviews reveal most of the recurring problems.
cards.example: Tell me about the last time you looked for a plumber: where did you search first?
alts: A one to one talk about what a buyer actually did in the past, rather than what they think they might do.

cards.definition: How likely are you to recommend us, from 0 to 10? Promoters answer 9 or 10, passives 7 or 8, detractors 0 to 6. NPS = percentage of promoters minus percentage of detractors, from minus 100 to plus 100.
cards.example: 50 percent promoters, 30 percent passives and 20 percent detractors give an NPS of 30.
alts: Share of customers scoring 9 or 10 minus share scoring 0 to 6 on how likely they are to recommend, from minus 100 to plus 100.

exercises.prompt: You want to know WHY customers cancel their subscription. Which method first?
choices: Qualitative interviews with people who cancelled
A survey of 5,000 random French adults
Counting cancellations per month in a chart
Reading the annual report of a competitor
exercises.explain: Why questions need qualitative research. Once you know the reasons, a quantitative survey can measure how common each one is.

variants.prompt: You want to know what share of customers cancel because of price. Which method?
choices: A quantitative survey of a large sample
Three interviews with friends
A single focus group of 8 people
Reading one online review

variants.prompt: Which research best explores the words customers use about a problem?
choices: Qualitative interviews
A large quantitative survey
Counting website visits
Analysing the ad budget

exercises.prompt: A report from an industry association that you reuse is which kind of data?
choices: Secondary data
Primary data
First-party data
Qualitative data
exercises.explain: Secondary data was collected by someone else for another purpose. It is cheap and fast; check its date and method.

variants.prompt: A survey you design and run on your own customers produces which kind of data?
choices: Primary data
Secondary data
Third-party data
Public data

variants.prompt: Which of these is secondary data?
choices: Official statistics from INSEE
Interviews you run with clients
A survey you sent last week
A test you ran on your site
Do you agree that our great new app is easier?
How often did you use the app last week?
Which feature did you use most recently?
What did you do before using the app?
exercises.explain: A leading question suggests the answer. Neutral questions about facts and past behaviour give more reliable data.

variants.prompt: Which question is neutral?
choices: How often did you use the app last week?
Do you agree our app is the best one?
How much do you love our new design?
Would you not prefer our cheaper plan?

variants.prompt: Why is Do you agree that our great new app is easier a bad survey question?
choices: It suggests the answer it wants
It is too short to understand
It asks about the past
It uses a rating scale

exercises.prompt: When people say they would buy a product, sales will match their answers closely.
exercises.explain: False. Stated intentions overestimate real behaviour, especially for virtuous products. Prefer observed behaviour: pre-orders, tests, real sales.

variants.prompt: Pre-orders are a more reliable signal of demand than survey answers about buying intentions.
variants.explain: True. Paying, even a deposit, is behaviour. Saying yes in a survey costs nothing.

variants.prompt: People predict their own future purchases accurately in surveys.
variants.explain: False. Stated intentions overestimate real behaviour, especially for virtuous or new products.

exercises.prompt: A focus group of 8 people loves your concept. What can you conclude?
choices: The concept is worth testing on a larger sample
80 percent of the market will buy the product
The launch is certain to be a success
There is no need for further research
exercises.explain: A focus group explores; it does not measure. Eight people cannot represent a market.

variants.prompt: What is a focus group good for?
choices: Exploring perceptions and the words people use
Measuring the market share of a brand
Predicting the exact sales of a launch
Replacing all other research

variants.prompt: Why should a focus group never be used to measure?
choices: Too few people, swayed by the loudest ones
It is illegal to count the answers
People are paid to lie in them
It only works in B2B markets

exercises.prompt: Your NPS survey gets 60 percent promoters, 25 percent passives and 15 percent detractors. What is the NPS?
exercises.explain: NPS = promoters minus detractors = 60 minus 15 = 45. Passives count in the total but not in the subtraction.

variants.prompt: 50 percent promoters, 20 percent passives, 30 percent detractors. What is the NPS?
40 percent promoters, 40 percent passives and 20 percent detractors. What is the NPS?

exercises.prompt: A customer gives 7 out of 10 to the recommendation question. Which group is it in?
choices: Passive
Promoter
Detractor
Neutral promoter
exercises.explain: Only 9 and 10 are promoters, 0 to 6 are detractors, 7 and 8 are passives.

variants.prompt: A customer answers 6 to the recommendation question. Which group is it in?
choices: Detractor
Passive
Promoter
Neutral

variants.prompt: Which scores make a promoter?
choices: 9 and 10
7 and 8
8 to 10
6 to 10

exercises.prompt: After a support chat, you ask: how easy was it to solve your issue? Which metric is it?
choices: CES
NPS
CSAT
ROAS
exercises.explain: Customer Effort Score measures effort. Low effort predicts loyalty well after service interactions.

variants.prompt: After a purchase you ask: how satisfied are you with your order? Which metric?
choices: CSAT
CES
NPS
CAC

variants.prompt: Which question measures NPS?
choices: How likely are you to recommend us?
How easy was it to solve your issue?
How satisfied are you with this order?
How much did you spend this year?

exercises.prompt: Which interview question gives the most reliable insight?
choices: Tell me about the last time you bought running shoes
Would you pay 150 euros for smart shoes?
Do you like our new shoe design?
What features should the perfect shoe have?
exercises.explain: Past behaviour is fact; predictions and opinions are guesses. The Mom Test principle: ask about their life, not your idea.

variants.prompt: Which interview question follows the Mom Test?
choices: What did you do the last time this happened?
Would you use an app that solves this?
Do you think our idea is good?
How much would you pay for it?

variants.prompt: Why ask about past behaviour rather than future intentions?
choices: Past behaviour is fact; predictions are guesses
People remember the future better
The law forbids questions about the future
Past questions are quicker to ask

exercises.prompt: Why can 1,000 well chosen people describe the opinion of a whole country?
choices: A representative sample mirrors the population structure
Every French adult answered in the past
The law requires polls to be accurate
People in big cities speak for the rest
exercises.explain: Representativeness matters more than size. A biased sample of 100,000 can be wrong where 1,000 quota-based answers are right.

variants.prompt: A survey of 100,000 readers of one magazine predicts an election badly. Why?
choices: The sample is big but not representative
100,000 answers is far too few
The answers were never counted
Elections cannot be studied at all

variants.prompt: What matters more than sample size for a reliable poll?
choices: Representativeness of the sample
The length of the questionnaire
The colour of the survey form
The day of the week it is sent

exercises.prompt: Put a research project in order.
steps: Write the business decision the research must inform
Read existing secondary data on the subject
Run a few qualitative interviews to find the themes
Measure the themes with a quantitative survey
Decide and share the findings with the team
exercises.explain: Start from the decision, use what exists, explore, measure, then act. Research with no decision attached ends up in a drawer.
